claims.text: Adding a controlled amount of an additional alloying element enhances superconductivity in a high-entropy alloy.
The additional alloying element modifies the alloy's local electronic structure and electron–phonon coupling.
The additional element increases the density of states at the Fermi level.
An increased density of states at the Fermi level strengthens the superconducting pairing interaction.
The baseline material is a stable equiatomic high-entropy alloy containing at least five elements and exhibiting a superconducting transition temperature.
The intervention is addition of 1–5 atomic percent of a designated alloying element.
The added element changes local chemical disorder.
The added element changes the local density of electronic states.
The added element may alter phonon modes.
The added element creates localized regions with enhanced electronic density at the Fermi level.
The electronic and electron–phonon changes promote stronger Cooper pairing.
The modified alloy will have a measurably higher superconducting transition temperature than the unmodified baseline.
The beneficial effect is expected only below approximately 5 atomic percent addition, provided that crystal structure and phase stability are preserved.
Higher additions may cause structural degradation or phase separation that negates beneficial electronic effects.
Local strain, electron scattering, and phonon-mode variation may also influence the superconducting transition temperature.
A concentration series at 0%, 1%, 3%, and 5% addition can test the proposed concentration dependence.
Absence of a systematic increase in transition temperature or electronic density of states would falsify the proposed enhancement mechanism.

contradictions.description: The intervention and experiment include a 5 atomic percent sample, whereas the boundary states that the effect is expected only below 5 atomic percent.

Loss of structural integrity is defined as outside the hypothesis's boundary conditions, but the falsification rule also treats structural compromise as falsifying the mechanism rather than as an excluded test condition.
